content: Facing the World is a charitable organization based in the United Kingdom that provides surgical interventions for children suffering from severe facial disfigurements. These children are primarily from economically disadvantaged countries where access to specialized surgical care is unavailable. The charity aims to address both the functional impairments and the profound emotional and psychological trauma caused by these conditions, often exacerbated by societal stigma. The organization was founded in 2003 by Norman Waterhouse and Martin Kelly, two craniofacial plastic surgeons affiliated with Chelsea and Westminster Hospital. Both founders had previously volunteered their expertise with international medical outreach programs but were deeply affected by the cases they encountered in resource-limited settings, where inadequate facilities and a lack of specialized expertise prevented them from providing the necessary care. Recognizing these limitations, they established Facing the World to bring children to the UK for surgery, leveraging the advanced medical infrastructure and the expertise of like-minded UK-based medical professionals. To manage the charity, Sarah Driver-Jowitt was appointed, and in 2004, an office was set up near London hospitals where most of the surgeries are performed. The charity was officially launched on February 15, 2003, during a fundraising premiere of the film Solaris, attended by George Clooney and his co-stars. The charity’s operations involve identifying children with severe facial deformities in their home countries. These deformities often result in significant functional challenges or emotional distress due to community stigma. The children undergo an initial assessment in their home country to determine whether surgical intervention is feasible and to identify the specific care required. If deemed suitable, arrangements are made to transport the child to London for treatment. The medical team donates their services, while the charity relies on fundraising and donations to cover additional medical costs, travel, and accommodation for the child and a guardian. Facing the World gained public attention through a Channel 4 documentary titled My New Face, which aired on November 15, 2006. The hour-long program documented the charity’s work over a year and highlighted several cases. These included Arianto from Jakarta, who suffered from facial gigantism caused by neurofibromatosis; Ney, a Cambodian boy born with encephalocele, a condition where part of the brain protrudes through a skull defect into the face; Zaynab, an eight-month-old girl from Gaza with a cleft palate and harelip; and Eyerusalem from Addis Ababa, one of the charity’s earliest patients, who underwent surgery in 2003 to remove a vascular malformation.
